#1934. Guiseley v Sutton United: Juggling FA Cup and league is not an issue for Lions

Just over a year after the PE teacher took charge at Nethermoor Park, the Lions are third in the Northern Premier League Premier Division. Beating Sutton United on Saturday goes hand in hand with the league.

It is easy to see why Richards is such a fan of the world's most famous domestic cup competition.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

"I don't like 'This isn't our priority this year,'" says Richards. "I might make a couple of changes with personnel, but we've built a squad where one in, one out, the quality doesn't change.

"We've had a county cup game within this (period between the qualifying rounds and Saturday) and played a team three leagues below us, but I still took a strong side. We won that 4-0. It's really important to get a clean sheet.

"We had a game against Leek Town on Tuesday in the league, and in line with the laws, they said they would postpone it if we wished. But we wanted to play it.

"It could have easily been one where players were subconsciously or consciously not at it 100 per cent. We ran out comfortable 4-1 winners and managed to get all five subs on. We came out with no new injuries.

"The players are in really good form. We've won eight and drawn one of our last nine games."

The Football Association have put attractive prize money into the early stages of their blue riband competition, giving something for romantics and pragmatists to play for. Victory on Saturday is worth £47,750, but even losing will bring in £15,800, and there is minimum prize money of £21,200 in round two.

"We're expecting a big crowd," said Richards. "There's never been that pressure from the club, but we have to be aware of prize money. If you want to improve the ground or reinvest in the squad, it's excellent.

"We got 1,600 at the (third qualifying round) Bradford (Park Avenue) game. "Then we played Leiston away and even though the gate money wasn't huge, it did give us publicity.

"And it's memories for the players. When I was at Halifax Town I got as far as the second round (in 1999). We lost in a replay to Reading. I remember Darren Caskey scoring the penalty at the Madejski Stadium, which was very new.

"As a manager, I've taken my two previous clubs (Stocksbridge Park Steels and Penistone Church) the furthest they've ever been in the FA Cup. The players still talk about that.

"I think this is the 11th time in Guiseley’s 117-year history they've got to the first round. They've only got to the second round twice and they were a National League side.

"Hopefully if there's new supporters coming, they may come back for two, three, four more games.

"There's a backlog of games, but winning builds momentum."

Playing a South London team from the Conference brings challenges for a part-time club, but nothing Richards is afraid of.

"I'm doing my research on Sutton," he says. "We'll train as we would do for any other game. But there'll be over 2,000 watching so we've got to use that as a motivation.

"Our head of football watches as many games as he can, so he went to Sutton against Harrogate Town. I've not been able to watch them live but I've got plenty of footage.

"They've got some real pace and power in wide areas. They've got good footballers in attacking midfield, but they are quite direct.

"Their pitch is an excellent surface, so they do try and play when they can, but they're quite happy to go forward very quickly.

"If I was playing a team two leagues below, I'd try and play on the front foot so we'll expect them to get the ball forward quickly and really commit numbers forward."

"We get school holidays, so that's the time I spend with my family," he says. "When you're doing well, it can get even busier, but I can't complain.

"I'm the vice-principal at Penistone Grammar School and I teach A-Level PE. It's my 12th year.

"I live in a little village called Shepley. We train at Lightcliffe Academy, about half-an-hour away.

"Midweek games are a bit of a nightmare with traffic, but my coach lives around the corner and my assistant lives in Thorpe Hesley so we're always travelling together.

"My pupils aren't fully aware of Guiseley but know the level it's at and what I do. We also have a number of teaching staff who follow non-league football. A few are going."

And whenever this run ends, it will be back to pushing for promotion from the seventh tier. They are three points behind leaders Redcar Athletic with a game in hand.

"When we took over at the end of October (2025), they were out of every competition and third from bottom," recalls Richards. "My objective was, at this stage, to be in every competition and above two points per game and we've achieved that.

"Only one goes up automatically but there are now six play-off places. We've got to make sure iIf we don't win it, we fall into a high play-off position."

Then this experience of knockout football will come in handy.

"With my previous clubs, we won promotions in the play-offs," he points out. "Even though at the time you're not thinking about it, I can reference the cup wins as I give my teamtalk.

"It's a long season, so every little bit helps."

#1931. St Mirren 0 Rangers 2: Winless away run ended with comfortable victory for Ibrox side

Rangers banished their recent away day blues with a solid 2-0 win over St Mirren in Paisley.

Draws against Dundee and Hearts in their last two William Hill Premiership games away from Ibrox had blemished the Gers’ focused title challenge, but Derek McInnes’s side were determined to leave The Marbill Coaches Stadium without a mark on them.

In-form striker Ryan Naderi scored with a soft penalty after 18 minutes before returning skipper Dan Neil added a second just after the hour mark with a deflected strike to extend the Light Blues’ unbeaten run in all competitions to 12 games.

Rangers moved to within one point of leaders Celtic having played the same number of fixtures, albeit the Hoops can can restore their four-point lead against Kilmarnock at Celtic Park on Sunday before the the international break gives the league another breather.

The unusual 8pm kick off on a Saturday night added atmosphere to the evening. St Mirren boss Craig McLeish made five changes, with Declan John, Louis Jackson, Samuel Ramos, Ismeal Kabia and Jake Young all coming in while Neil replaced Tuur Rommens and James Penrice dropped to left-back.

Amid a hurly-burly start to the game, Buddies keeper Jacob Chapman saved an early effort from Rangers wide-man Badredine Bouananai, then in the 12th minute made a crucial block from Naderi, who latched on to a Kevin Kelsy header, at the expense of a corner which came to nothing.

However, the big striker soon made amends.

Back-tracking St Mirren attacker Ramos was far from happy when referee Nick Walsh pointed to the spot following his challenge on Penrice just inside the box, after the Gers defender had raced 60 yards to back up the Light Blues’ South Korea international attacker Kim Min-su.

It looked like there had been little contact but a VAR check confirmed the penalty and Naderi, with a stuttering run up, casually sent Chapman the wrong way with his spot-kick for his ninth goal of the season.

The aggrieved home side fought furiously to get back on level terms and on a counter after 37 minutes, Ramos tested visiting keeper Ivor Pandur with a decent drive from the edge of the box, before Jake Young fired a shot high over the bar.

In a sprightly start to the second half, with Kim showing some delightful touches around the St Mirren penalty area, Kelsy drove wide of the far post from 16 yards.

Then, in the 54th minute, Kim set up Kelsy but Chapman brilliantly deflected the close-range dink and the home side got the ball to safety before the stretching Kelsy could not connect properly with a cross from midfielder Nicolas Raskin.

However, the visitors eventually got the second when another swift attack ended with the ball coming out to Neil, whose shot came off St Mirren defender Louis Jackson and ended up in the back of the net.

St Mirren kept battling and Pandur made a terrific save from substitute Eseosa Sule’s strike from a Declan John cross.

The Rangers keeper then denied another St Mirren replacement, Luke Thomas, before Saints defender Calvin Ramsay headed against the outside of the post from the rebound, and that was effectively the end of St Mirren’ possible comeback.

"Especially this night, we were not at this level at all, and if you are not compact, if you are shuffling, especially when they try to play around you to pull you out of your position, they will use all these gaps between your players, because they recognise this immediately," said Jakirovic.

"Our mental resilience is very important because of everything we did in the past – this team, together, chemistry, togetherness, team spirit, everything. So this is the main thing we have."

Asked what he would talk to Mikel Arteta about if he shares a drink with the Gunners manager at full-time, Jakirovic replied: "I will ask him to give me his budget!

"But he deserves to be at this level. He was (a coach) at Man City, now he's been at Arsenal (as manager) almost seven years, and it's progress every year.

"It's not easy to build a new team, but you have options to add more quality in your team, because Arsenal is a top-five team in Europe, in terms of everything.

"This a chance to show we can compete there. Maybe you can surprise them with something, and also you can compare where we are right now, because they are the best, it's not a secret."

#1924. Leeds United v Tottenham Hotspur: Daniel Farke on 'elite' duo on opposing sides at Elland Road

Something else sets them apart from their contemporaries.

It was brought into sharp focus by Harry Kane's recent elevation to Ballon d'Or winner amid a glittering ceremony in his home city of London.

Kane's staggering goalscoring numbers and consistency speaks for itself, but it hardly happened overnight.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

What sets him apart is his elite mentality from an early age. 'Work hard in silence. Let success be your noise' was his social media post after being named as the best footballer in the world.

For all his trappings and status, no one could ever describe him as narcissistic.

That message might just resonate with two players on opposing sides today: Archie Gray and James Trafford.

The former, of course, is well known to Leeds United supporters. In an ideal world, he will still be stepping out in the white of Leeds and not Tottenham Hotspur.

It's hard to believe that Gray is still not yet 21 - that milestone arrives in March.

He is part-way through his third season in the Premier League and fourth campaign as a first-teamer. He is not far shy of 150 competitive games already in a career which is surely only going one way.

Capable of playing centre-back, full-back and midfield, he is a manager's dream. Tactically adept, responsible and mature beyond his years, it's easy to see that he belongs to a revered football dynasty.

He is also driven, football-obsessed and low-maintenance. The sort of person - and not just player - that Daniel Farke likes. Even if he will not be wanting to see any of his acumen today.

Farke said: "It was early to see (his elite mentality). When Archie came through at the age of 17, he replaced my vice-captain and our club legend Luke Ayling.

"It was not an easy decision. It was not for the dressing room. I came in as the new coach and I've got a club legend. Together with Liam Cooper, he was wearing the captain's armband.

"But he was on the bench because I played Archie, a 17-year-old kid. But Archie had already at this age more or less this mentality and the quality. He was a different drawer (top-drawer).

"The same when I played him in midfield - you had experienced players like Glen Kamara, for example, out for his position. But just due to the quality and mentality that (Gray) he had meant he was ready and prepared to play on a Championship level.

"I think he has also sometimes worn the captain's armband for Tottenham at a more prominent level.

"It says a lot about him and you need this quality and mentality if you want to be there as a young player playing so many games on this level."

As with Kane, Gray has had to handle knockbacks - being part of a Spurs side that has flirted with relegation in the past few seasons. It's something that Leeds and England goalkeeper Trafford also knows a fair bit about.

The 24-year-old heads into the game on the back of a howler in last weekend's loss to Bournemouth - gifting a goal to Cherries player Evanilson.

He was also culpable—though by no means as damningly - for Riccardo Calafiori's goal in United's 2-1 reverse at Arsenal on October 10.

Mistakes are - and will forever remain - an omnipresent part of a goalkeeper's life.

Trafford also currently has the best save percentage in the Premier League at 80.5. Only Hull City's Konstantinos Tzolakis - with 32 saves - has stopped more shots so far this term.

So the Cumbrian, from a humble farming roots near Cockermouth, has plenty to shout about if he cares to. Which he doesn't.

Farke said: "He's really top. James has delivered top performances for us so far.

"He was, of course, involved in the first goal (at Bournemouth) and sadly in this case it was then decisive, but that's also what you have to deal with, especially as a young player and young goalkeeper.

"You deal with these setbacks and learn from them and it's quite important for me that he didn't look shy of confidence during this week.

"He was there with his normal performance. I'm pretty sure he has also learned from it, but for me it's also important that he doesn't lose his confidence and his rhythm. Of course, he will be in goal and also hopefully with an important display."

Speaking of statistics, Leeds head into the game in receipt of an unwanted Premier League record: they have not won a top-flight game played before 3pm on a Saturday in 21 attempts since March 2022.

Ending that statistic would be a nice way to head into an international break, not that Farke is losing any sleep over it.

"I wouldn't take too much into the timing', the German opined.

"I think it's also normal. In the last years we were on Premier League level, we've spent more or less all the time in the relegation pattern, so it's less likely to win games in comparison to Man City or Liverpool or Arsenal right now. It's another chance to break the record, it's important to be switched on."

Keane left before the 2026-27 campaign, and he was replaced by Balazs Borbely who came from Gyor ETO, the club that have been one of the surprise packages in recent years, even winning the Nemzeti Bajnokság I (league title) last season.

It was quite a quiet summer for the Budapest-based team, as their big splash was Veljko Birmancevic from Sparta Praha for €2m. Matus Bero and Nathan Zohore arrived on free transfers, while Adam Nagy joined for a low fee from Spezia.

An away win against Celtic kicked off their league phase, following by victories against Viktoria Plzen and Torreense. Overall, the Hungarian outfit have scored nine times and have conceded just three in what has been a perfect start in the UEL.

Ferencvaros’ only defeat came in their league debut on July 26 (2-4 against Baksi FC). Since then, they have gone on a long unbeaten streak of five wins and five draws, climbing to third place, just two points behind league leaders Gyor and with a game in hand.

In terms of injury news, the visitors will be missing Slovakian midfielder Matus Bero, while Bence Otvos is recovering from an ACL injury and will not take part. Aside from that, they have a clean bill of health.

Borbely’s side have so far alternated between a 4-1-4-1 formation – deploying former Liverpool player Nabi Keita or Adamy Nagy (who played for Bologna and Spezia) as midfielders – and a 4-2-3-1 to offer a bit more width.

A few rotations are expected from the weekend’s game – where they cruised to a 2-0 win – and the first set comes in defence. Radnoti, Nagy, Zohore and O’Dowda are all expected to return to the starting XI, with Gomez being the only survivor to retain his place.

Maiga will find a new partner at the base of the midfield in the aforementioned Nagy, whilst Zachariassen will start ahead of them.

On the wings, it’s an unchanged set-up with leading goalscorer Zachariassen and Birmancevic starting. Then, Yusuf is expected to return to the starting XI.

#1918. Defiant Bruno Fernandes claims he wasn't dropped for publicly criticising Michael Carrick - and hits out at 'a lot of lies' in sweary interview after Man United's stunning 3-2 comeback against Roma

By WILL GRIFFEE and CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER

Published: 17:42 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 20:12 EDT, 3 November 2026

Bruno Fernandes launched into an adrenaline-fuelled, X-rated rant after Man United's stunning comeback win over Roma on Tuesday night.

Having been at the centre of the storm surrounding the club's abysmal form and his undermining of manager Michael Carrick, Fernandes offered contrition for publicly criticising tactics but denied it was the reason he was dropped last week.

The club captain was benched by Carrick for United's 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth before being reintegrated against Chelsea and Roma, winning Man of the Match and scoring against the Italians.

Amazon Prime presenter Gabby Logan was forced to apologise for Fernandes' bad language after he let the emotion pour out of him in the post-match interview.

The stirring 3-2 comeback at Old Trafford on Tuesday night was the jumping-off point for Fernandes to unburden himself, saying: 'We don't need to save anyone's job.

'The club needed that win. The players needed that win. It is something we needed as a group of players and staff.

'We have been working so hard to get out of this situation together. It has been tough. There has been a lot of speculation in the media.

"Carrick was right" 🔴👏Bruno Fernandes gave an open, honest assessment after United's 3-2 win over Roma 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/QAWDt6VXQr

Bruno Fernandes gave a passionate interview after starring in Man United's 3-2 win

'A lot of lies around many things that have happened at this club, between me and the manager, like that we have cleared the air. Nothing like that happened.

'The manager took a decision of making myself on the bench because I wasn't performing. And that's fair.

'Everyone felt like that was a punishment for the words that I had [after Como]. And if it was, it was right.

'The manager makes the decisions. I have to accept it. I have to go forward with that. It doesn't change the belief I have in the manager, the staff and every player at this club.

'And it doesn't change my aim to win every f***ing game that I have ahead of me.'

Carrick was given a stay of execution by club bosses at United after losing against Bournemouth when he seemed destined to be sacked.

Defeat at Chelsea appeared to push him closer to the exit door but Fernandes and Co fought back from 2-0 down on Tuesday night to give their boss and a beleaguered fanbase a much-needed lift.

Fernandes, along with Lisandro Martinez, had both publicly criticised different aspects of the club, with the Argentine targeting Jason Wilcox and Fernandes making disparaging comments about Carrick's tactics.

Michael Carrick and Fernandes embraced after the Portuguese came off at Old Trafford

Fernandes was overcome with emotion after United sealed the memorable comeback

His post-Como interview was widely condemned by fans and pundits alike, with Garry Neville lamenting: 'If that's your captain saying that, imagine what they're saying in the dressing room behind closed doors when no one's listening. That's horrific.'

He also told Fernandes to 'read the room' and accused him of being an 'excuse merchant' on his podcast.

'He's gone and basically thrown his manager under the bus the week after [Lisandro] Martinez did the same,' he said.

'So get in your box. You know where you stand. Michael Carrick's won things for the football club on a constant basis, and proven that he can have the humility, the resilience. And Bruno has got that. Bruno has delivered for Manchester United in more ways than any other player in the last 13 years.

'He's massively talented but he let himself down this week. He didn't need to do that because he's basically stuck the knife into his manager.'

Fernandes and the United players were booed by the United fans after the Bournemouth debacle, while Carrick was given a warm reception, clearly indicating where the supporter sentiment fell.

But the mood was altogether different on Tuesday night. Roma raced to a 2-0 lead in what appeared to be another United evening of despair.

Then Fernandes netted a re-taken penalty before two late Matheus Cunha goals snatched a crucial victory.

Afterwards, Carrick reflected: 'This place does it (inspires comebacks). No matter what situation you're in, how tough it can seem, the supporters are desperate to get behind you and we gave them something to go on.

Carrick's job was hanging by a thread but he has given himself some breathing room

'I’m proud of everyone pulling through in a tough situation. I don’t like talking to the lads too much about the history of this place, but it’s magical. There’s something when we have these nights and we do it the hard way, and one moment can flip the whole feeling.

‘It’s one win so we’re not getting too carried away, but it was an important one for us.’

When asked about his future at the club, he added: 'I don't have a crystal ball to know what happens next.

'We move on to the weekend, we've got a really important game here against Aston Villa, which we need to prepare for right.'

Youri Tielemans played a part in the sensational turnaround after coming on as a substitute for Carlos Baleba when United’s £70million summer signing pulled his right hamstring at the start of the second half.

Tielemans said of Carrick: ‘There has been a lot of pressure on him and that’s how we repay him, with a comeback like this. Big character, big fight.’

Asked if the victory might save the head coach’s job, the Belgian replied: ‘That's a different question. The only thing we can do is stick behind him, fight for him and fight for the club.

‘Let's hope this is a good turnaround for us and we can build on this.’

#1916. Rangers' Iron man of Ibrox always turned up - and should always be remembered

When Rangers TV released a short film about Harold Davis, the former Rangers player and war hero, on YouTube at the end of last month, the idea was to allow an important tribute to reach a wider audience.

It’s hard to imagine they could have predicted the initial interest. The mini documentary from RTV Studios has already attracted over 10,000 views. It is well on the way to the 100,000 (and counting) audience for a similarly essential homage to Davie Cooper to mark last year’s 30th anniversary of the wondrously talented winger’s dreadfully premature death.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Familiarise yourself with a tale of derring-do that ought to be turned into a blockbuster. It contains all the ingredients. Davis was in the process of establishing himself as a footballer with East Fife before National Service took him to Fort George, the Black Watch’s regimental base near Inverness, and then to the ‘forgotten war’ in Korea.

According to a telegram delivered to his parents’ house in Perth, “Corporal Harold Davis” was placed on the “dangerously ill” list after being gunned down at the Hook – a ridge around which much of the intense fighting took place – in May 1953.

As well as multiple stomach wounds, he sustained a shattered heel bone. A return to football seemed out of the question but after more than two years of rehabilitation, Scott Symon, his old East Fife manager, signed Davis for Rangers.

His incredible story certainly deserves a wider audience. I have to declare an interest because it’s now 20 years, almost to the day, since my then sports editor handed me an assignment that still ranks among the most memorable of my time in journalism. I was tasked with interviewing Davis for this newspaper.

Like so many things worth doing, it wasn’t a straightforward mission. We had to track Harold down first. Last heard of running a hotel in Gairloch, he had since moved with his wife Vi to Badachro, a small fishing village outside the Wester Ross town.

I drew up outside his beautiful home and sat rapt for hours in his company. When I made moves to leave – after all, a near five-hour drive back to Edinburgh loomed – I was instructed to stay the night. I did what I was told. Nobody disobeyed Harold – or Vi for that matter.

Another place was set at the dinner table and then we sat and watched the League Cup quarter-final between Hibs and Hearts while awaiting updates from Ibrox as Paul Le Guen’s Rangers hosted St Johnstone. A 2-0 home defeat underlined where the Ibrox side were at the time and prompted evident grumbles of disgust from the direction of Harold's chair.

The piece, when it appeared, was headlined: “The forgotten hero of a forgotten war". Harold isn’t forgotten now but it did seem like he was forgotten then. Not, I accept, by knowledgeable Rangers fans of a certain age, who recognised his distinction in bridging two eras.

When the right-half joined Rangers in 1956 he played with George Young, Ian McColl, Alex Scott and Johnny Hubbard. When he finished eight years later the likes of John Greig, Jim Baxter and Willie Henderson were in the team with him. He bridged two great eras and won four league championship medals, two League Cups and a Scottish Cup.

The medals are back on display at Ibrox. “Harold’s son Alan sold the medals to raise money for a local kids’ charity in the Gairloch area which unfortunately meant they were leaving Ibrox where they had been on display in the museum,” reports Tom Clark, a friend.

“But the wonderful news is that the buyer who bought them did not want the Rangers fans to miss out on seeing them and loaned them back to Rangers. They are now back in the exact same position where they were. So you have the double bonus of the medals being back on display and children benefitting in Harold’s name.”

Davis was a modest man but there was one claim he made on behalf of himself that sticks in my mind and remains true to this day.

“I might not have been the best player who ever put on a blue jersey,” he told me as the low winter sun dipped into Gairloch Bay. “But not one person who has put on a blue jersey started below where I had been in a physical sense and managed to reach the heights I did.”

It’s why he was so affronted by Jim Baxter’s casual attitude and tendency to turn up for games with the smell of the booze from the previous night – or from earlier the same day – still on his breath. He never toned down his disdain for his talented but wayward old teammate, whom he once pinned against an Ibrox dressing-room wall for some on-field insolence.

Rangers had no finer ambassador than Davis, who was delighted to be offered the honorary life president position of the Rangers Supporters Erskine Appeal (RSEA). This charity, founded by Clark to support Erskine homes for ex-service men and women, celebrates its 20th anniversary early next year and has raised £1.7 million to date.

It goes from strength to strength and remains inspired by Davis, who died eight years ago at the age of 85.

A chair is left empty at fund-raising dinners for both him and Vi, who passed away in 2023. It’s a deserved and poignant gesture but one that might cause Harold to smile. Being 'empty-chaired’ is a horrible modern term denoting those who haven’t contributed or haven’t turned up.

The Iron man of Ibrox always, always turned up. His contribution, while immense to Rangers, extended far beyond the club and merits the gratitude of all.

#1913. Celtic star's telepathic connection with strike partner and why his best is yet to come

Callum Osmand continues to highlight his considerable potential by making his mark at Celtic, but the young forward is adamant that what supporters have witnessed so far is only the beginning.

The 20-year-old has experienced a whirlwind introduction to first-team football in Glasgow, with the demands of competing for a place at one of Scotland's biggest clubs providing a steep learning curve. Yet his decisive contribution to Celtic's dramatic 3-2 Europa League victory over Besiktas offered another glimpse of the qualities that have made him such an intriguing prospect.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Introduced by Martin O’Neill in the second half, Osmand wasted little time making his presence felt against the Turkish side, scoring just 43 seconds after coming on before delivering a perfectly weighted pass for Camilo Duran to complete his double. His impact transformed the contest and secured Celtic a much-needed victory.

“Yeah, it was crazy. It's a surreal feeling when it's my first touch as well,” he reflected. “I was a bit nervous that I'd shanked it, but no, I'm happy that I caught it nicely. He (O’Neill) knows that I know what he expects from me, so it was about making sure I can come and bring some energy.”

His burgeoning partnership with Duran was another highlight. Their understanding was evident in the build-up to Celtic's vital third goal, with the former Fulham forward displaying excellent vision to pick out the Colombian's run in behind.

“I thought he was offside, to be honest!” Osmand admitted. “I was looking at the bench saying 'Close?', and they were like, 'Yeah, it's tight', but I know where he's going. He's such a sharp striker, so I know if I put that in the space, the keeper is not getting anywhere near it. He's a top, top player, so I can't fault him at all.”

Their connection is extending beyond the pitch, too. Despite a language barrier, Osmand feels the pair have struck up a genuine friendship.

“His English is really not great, but somehow we manage to talk to each other a lot,” he laughed. “I think I find him quite a good friend of mine now. Although we might not speak many words, you can tell just by looking. We talk to each other a lot. Maybe it's little words, but we get on really well.

“Camilo is unbelievable, a really top player. You can see even by the way he walks and the way he moves. I learn off him every day. He's a great guy.”

The victory over Besiktas could prove pivotal to Celtic's European ambitions, and Osmand hopes it will provide the confidence required to approach the remaining fixtures with greater freedom.

“For us, it felt like a must-win. That was our mindset going into the game and it’s a huge result,” he explained. “We knew we could still qualify, but we knew we had to get something out of Thursday night, and I think the boys done amazing.

“Sometimes when you're not as confident, it's tough to play the football you want to play, but as you can see, when we're confident, it just goes forward every time. We know when we're not playing as well, and we'll be the first, as players, to critique each other and critique ourselves before anyone else. It is about just staying together, building and getting a result like this to take into the next game.”

Osmand is equally candid about his own development, insisting there is still plenty of room for improvement despite his encouraging start. He pointed out what will be key to taking his game to the next level.

“I'm nowhere near where I want to be personally, and there's stuff I need to tidy up on, like decision-making and all this stuff,” Osmand admitted. “But I feel like the more games I play, the more I understand and the more I learn. So on a personal note, that's what I want to do, just keep learning and keep understanding my role and obviously the players you're playing with.

“I've still only played a handful of games, so it's tough learning, but I feel like when you get thrown in the deep end, it's the best way to learn. It's just as long as I can get better every game, that's all I really want to focus on.”

His recent deployment on the left wing has also offered another opportunity to broaden his game. Although not a position he has traditionally occupied, Osmand is relishing the licence to express himself.

“I’m really enjoying it. It's a really fun position and it's very, very attacking,” he commented. “I have a lot of freedom and the staff give me that freedom and tell me to go and try and make something happen. It's a great feeling when you know you can just go and impose your game.”

#1909. Celtic vs Kilmarnock - prediction, team news, lineups

By Calum Burrowes | 06 Nov 2026 15:05, Last updated: 06 Nov 2026 20:38

Looking to move seven points clear at the top of the Scottish Premiership, Celtic return to league action on Sunday when they welcome Kilmarnock to Glasgow for their second meeting this season.

The Bhoys secured a dramatic second-half comeback victory over Besiktas in the Europa League during the week, while Killie head into this encounter on the back of a 2-2 draw with St Johnstone on Halloween.

After drawing with Dundee United and suffering their first defeat to Falkirk in nearly two decades, Martin O'Neill and his Celtic side went into their midweek clash with Turkish giants Besiktas in desperate need of a positive result, having dropped to second-bottom in the Europa League league-phase table.

The Bhoys produced a lacklustre first-half display at Celtic Park on Thursday night, managing just two touches in the opposition box during the opening 45 minutes. When they fell 1-0 behind shortly after the restart, it looked as though the Glasgow giants were heading for another disappointing European result.

However, substitutes Callum Osmand and Camilo Duran inspired a remarkable turnaround as Celtic took the lead, were pegged back in the 85th minute and then responded once again to secure a 3-2 victory over Vincenzo Italiano's side.

The three points provided a much-needed boost for O'Neill's men, whose lead at the top of the Scottish Premiership had been cut after collecting just one point from their previous two league outings.

Despite the demanding nature of their European comeback, the result could provide the confidence needed to spark an improvement in domestic performances.

Celtic currently hold a four-point advantage at the summit, although arch-rivals Rangers have a game in hand and could move above them if the Bhoys fail to return to winning ways on Sunday.

As for Kilmarnock, they travel to Glasgow seeking their first victory over Celtic since December 2023, having failed to win any of their previous 10 meetings with the Scottish champions.

Having finished third-bottom last season, Kilmarnock avoided the relegation playoffs with four consecutive victories to close out the 2025-26 campaign, but they would have been hoping to build on that strong finish rather than find themselves battling near the foot of the table again.

Under Neil McCann, who has won 36% of his matches since taking charge in January 2026, Kilmarnock have struggled for consistency and currently sit 11th in the 12-team division.

Two wins, three draws and seven defeats from their opening 12 matches have left McCann's side with just nine points, highlighting several areas that need to improve sooner rather than later.

Defensive frailties have been a particular concern, with Killie already conceding 28 goals at an average of 2.3 per game.

That is comfortably the worst defensive record in the Scottish Premiership, with second-highest Motherwell and St Mirren having shipped 20.

Celtic emerged from their European victory without any further injury concerns, although changes are likely after Duran and Osmand made an impact from the bench, with the former scoring twice and the latter also finding the net.

James Forrest and Sebastian Tounekti could be the players to make way, allowing both substitutes to earn starting roles.

Canadian full-back Alistair Johnston and Yang Hyun-Jun remain sidelined through injury, although both are expected to return in the coming weeks.

As for the visitors, McCann could stick with the same starting XI that drew 2-2 with 10-man St Johnstone as he looks to find some much-needed consistency.

Former Manchester United academy product Joe Hugill is expected to retain his place up front as he looks to build on the four goal involvements he has recorded this season.

McCann will be without Bailey Rice and Maksymillian Stryjek.

Johnstone; Lotomba, Carter-Vickers, Scales, Tierney; Nygren, McGregor, Baur; Duran, Hogh, Osmand

Manti; McCarthy, Deas, Stanger; Brandon, Tshibola, Lowery, Ring; Kiltie; Hugill, Daniels

Although Celtic have been inconsistent in recent weeks, their comeback victory over Besiktas should provide a timely confidence boost, and we expect them to return to winning ways in the league on Sunday.

Kilmarnock have looked particularly vulnerable defensively this season, and we believe the hosts will have enough attacking quality to exploit those weaknesses and secure a comfortable 3-0 victory.

#1907. Wolves loanee has no regrets about rocky Celtic ride as he steps out of shadows to embrace the spotlight

Sam Johnstone has experienced enough of football's highs and lows to understand that joining Celtic was never likely to be a straightforward undertaking.

But despite a turbulent introduction to life in Glasgow, the Wolves loanee insists he has absolutely no regrets about taking on one of the most demanding challenges of his career to date.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The former England international headed north of the border earlier this summer in search of regular first-team football and a fresh challenge. What followed has been a mixed introduction, with inconsistent results bringing added scrutiny, while adapting to a new team environment has required patience.

His career has been defined as much by patience as it has by perseverance. The Manchester United youth product has spent lengthy spells waiting in the wings for his opportunity, often occupying a back-up or third-choice role, while striving to establish himself as a No.1

Arriving at Celtic has offered a welcome change of circumstances. Rather than being confined to a supporting role, Johnstone has the chance to make the position between the sticks his own as he continues to enjoy a sustained run of games and remind people of the qualities that once earned him international recognition.

There is also the matter of developing relationships with the defenders in front of him. Communication, trust and familiarity are essential for any goalkeeper, and Johnstone recognises that those connections take time to establish.

“I think I've got to get used to them, they've got to get used to me, and that only happens through playing and through games. It's great to be in the team,” he said. “To get a run of games for any player, you find your rhythm. It was a new club for me, a new team, so that takes probably a couple of games to get used to as well.”

Having represented established clubs such as West Bromwich Albion and Crystal Palace, Johnstone is no stranger to pressure. However, he has discovered that the expectations at Celtic are particularly intense, arguably unlike anything he has experienced elsewhere in his career.

“Of course it has,” Johnstone admitted when asked whether fluctuating results had affected the mood within the dressing room. “I think the results affect it. This club's not used to losing, and we've probably lost too many games for this club.

“The expectation here, rightly so, is to win. Unfortunately, we hadn't quite met that expectation, and the lads know that. We all realise that, but we have to put things right in each game. It was tough. We're honest players, we're honest people, and honest with each other.”

Ultimately, though, signing for Celtic was an opportunity Johnstone was never likely to pass up. The quality within Martin O’Neill’s squad, coupled with the passion of the supporters and the chance to experience the club's unique atmosphere, made the move an attractive proposition.

“It's brilliant to play for this club,” he insisted. “The passion of the fans, good and bad. The standard of players on the pitch, day in, day out at training. When I came, I said I didn't have to think twice about coming here. It’s a great team to play in. The lads came up with the goods (on Thursday vs Besiktas], so we keep taking it game by game and go again on Sunday.”

Whether his time with the Scottish champions will provide the springboard to revitalise his career remains to be seen. Asked if the move had given him a fresh lease of life, Johnstone was typically measured in his response. “Let's see, let's see.”

#1906. The Dominik Szoboszlai dilemma: One of Europe's best midfielders who Liverpool must build around? Or a square peg who they play better without? This is what Andoni Iraola should do

Published: 21:00 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EDT, 3 November 2026

The folks in Liverpool’s commercial team devoted a fair portion of last season chasing after Dominik Szoboszlai.

As the club's player of the month more often than not, the Hungarian was obliged to fulfil a swathe of sponsorship duties and, like for many defenders last season, tying down Szoboszlai was not always easy. But he always completed these extracurricular activities, and was rewarded with a bumper new contract.

The midfielder was the standard-setter in pre-season and made vice-captain, with an eye on becoming the next man to wear the armband permanently when Virgil van Dijk eventually leaves. Szoboszlai’s role as protagonist continued in Andoni Iraola’s first competitive match with a last-gasp thunderous strike at Newcastle. Everything at Liverpool, it seemed, revolved around this handsome, chiseled star with a swagger.

Fast forward two months, however, and that's no longer the case. Szoboszlai has gone from first name on the teamsheet to having to fight for a starting spot. For some fans, he has become the scapegoat.

That seems wholly unfair but they point to the fact his half an hour from the bench against Arsenal coincided with Liverpool ceding control, balance and threat. Before that, Szoboszlai had missed four-and-a-half games – he went off injured early in a win at Brentford – and the Reds won all of them.

So, are Liverpool really better without the Hungarian? Let’s analyse both sides of the argument.

Would Andoni Iraola (right) really be better off without Dominik Szoboszlai (right)?

FOR: Drop him, he doesn’t fit Iraola’s system

The case against Szoboszlai revolves around balance, control and space.

Is it a coincidence that Florian Wirtz’s best run in a Liverpool shirt came in the last month, when the German had two midfielders behind him who were happy to do the defensive dirty work?

With both Szoboszlai and Wirtz in the side, it feels like the pair get in each other’s way and try to occupy the same positions, and Liverpool in turn are vulnerable to the counter-attack.

Alexis Mac Allister is enjoying his best form in well over a year and likes to arrive late into the box, but he cannot do this with Szoboszlai next to him as it leaves his team too exposed going the other way.

Young Trey Nyoni is a classy midfielder who thrives at dropping deep to start attacks and bait opposition presses. The 19-year-old is happy to sit back and allow those in front of him to thrive, such as Mac Allister playing a box-to-box role.

When Nyoni went off for Szoboszlai against Arsenal, Iraola’s side lost this balance and their chances of getting back into the game dwindled.

When Trey Nyoni went off for Szoboszlai against Arsenal, Iraola’s side lost this balance and their chances of getting back into the game dwindled

Szoboszlai is arrogant but has every right to be.

On his day, he is one of the best midfielders in Europe. A goal threat with one of the fiercest long shots in the game, with dead-ball precision, he is every bit the player Liverpool thought they were buying from RB Leipzig in 2023.

The midfielder has an engine akin to Declan Rice and is tireless in his work rate.

Surely, any team would want him and he is so talented that managers should build around him. As shown last term, he can win matches on his own. Despite his recent lay-off, he is barely injured and is a standard-bearer on the training pitch.

Iraola’s system is a 4-2-3-1 on paper but the Basque wants a bit of everything from his midfield: one No6, one No8 and one No10. Szoboszlai can play each of those roles. He has a tattoo of a Steven Gerrard quote and is the closest player to the former skipper that Anfield has seen since.

Internally, Liverpool believe Szoboszlai’s best years are ahead of him. In signing him up to a five-year deal at the end of last season – a process led by former sporting director Richard Hughes with the player’s agent Matyas Esterhazy – the Reds hierarchy were glad to stave off any future approaches from the likes of Real Madrid.

On his day, he is one of the best midfielders in Europe. Surely, any team would want him and he is so talented that managers should build around him

There are four solutions, two of which are outlined above: drop him and have a more balanced midfield or play him and benefit from his goal-scoring and creative powers, plus leadership and relentless running.

Another option may not be popular but there is a Wirtz-shaped elephant in the room. Does Iraola bench Wirtz and play Szoboszlai as the No10?

He’d have fewer defensive duties so the control and balance remains, but the Hungarian would pop up in dangerous areas to cause issues. Wirtz is a creative wizard when on form but how many times does he pass up an opportunity to shoot? Szoboszlai would already be wheeling away in celebration by the time Wirtz has made his mind up on what to do with an attack.

And then there is the compromise of Szoboszlai at right back. The player himself does not like it as he feels less important in that position, but it solves a lot of issues including all the aforementioned balance and control quirks. It also adds one thing that is bothering Iraola – creativity and attacking verve from right back.

The downside of this is Liverpool would lose the defensive acumen and physicality of aerial presence of Ronald Araujo, who is currently enjoying cult hero status at right back.

Szoboszlai is a strong right back but does not like playing there as he believes he has less influence on the game

The best teams build around the best players. There are always similar debates around Erling Haaland at Manchester City and anyone who argues the case to drop him is made to look silly.

So I will say the same about Szoboszlai. It is on Iraola to make it work. Most managers would kill for a depth of midfield talent like he has. Why not play him at right back? It solves multiple issues at once and Liverpool can finally replace the creativity Trent Alexander-Arnold used to bring from that role.

If Liverpool are seeing a game out, they can push Szoboszlai to the No 10, sub off Wirtz and bring on a true defender to help the physical battle.

Liverpool will be reunited with an old friend on Wednesday – and former cult hero Dirk Kuyt is relishing the chance to beat his old team.

Kuyt, played 285 times for the Reds between 2006 and 2012, scoring 71 times – and will face his old team for the first time on Wednesday as manager of Turkish giants Fenerbahce.

The Dutchman took over last week after a spell as assistant manager and said: ‘As soon as the draw was done, I was really excited because everyone knows how much Fenerbahce and Liverpool mean to me.

‘It will be a very special occasion for me but at the stage we're in, I'm not here for myself. I'm here for the club and that's what is important – to show the fans who deserve much more.

‘If we show up tomorrow with good energy, with passion and there to play, it can be a very special night.

‘Liverpool are an amazing team but so are Fenerbahce. If the fans show up, I think Europe will see how big this fan base is.’

Liverpool have happy memories in Istanbul having won this competition here in 2005 – though they lost twice to Galatasaray in Turkey last season, in the league phase and then last-16.

Fenerbahce play on the Asian side of the city and have familiar faces such as Romelu Lukaku, N'Golo Kante, Ederson, Nathan Ake and Mason Greenwood.

Liverpool will be without midfielder Ryan Gravenberch, who has a heel problem.

Boss Andoni Iraola said he liked a lot of the performance against Arsenal on Sunday but his side still need to improve.

‘It is difficult when you lose but honestly I am happy with a lot of things from the other day,’ he said. ‘I liked a lot of things but we still need to improve, especially attacking the box.'

#1904. Romano assesses ‘perfect’ derby win, the restart and Milan’s mercato targets: “A busy January”

Today, Fabrizio Romano has taken an in-depth look at AC Milan, their big weekend result and what’s next for the club.

After the Derby della Madonnina, there’s a very strong feeling surrounding Milan. All of a sudden, talk of winning a Scudetto under Ruben Amorim has gained genuine traction, and the group looks closer than ever.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

It’s not going to be easy, of course, but the Portuguese is obsessed with the idea of lifting the Serie A trophy with the Rossoneri, referencing as much in his press conference earlier today.

If that is going to happen this season, though, they will need to invest in January. After all, the squad remains shallow and extra support is very much needed.

Speaking to Time2Play.com, Romano looked at several things, including the derby and what the next few months could look like for the Diavolo.

“A derby can change the world. Because often, dynamics are triggered on and off the pitch, the atmosphere clears in an instant, and everyone contributes.

“AC Milan knows this well: a week ago, the home defeat against Bologna had brought much criticism, though it was also clearly the result of fatigue and significant absences, given the relentless pace of matches.

“But immediately afterwards, AC Milan set up their perfect derby—on and off the pitch, it’s no small matter—to build on and not just sit back.

“Because on the pitch, from Moreira to the usual Rabiot and Ruben Amorim, defended tooth and nail by Cardinale, everyone contributed that touch that led to the three points with a ferocious approach that became a winner.

“Off the pitch, Gerry Cardinale himself left his mark. Never like this.”

“The induction of legends during the week, Ricardo Kaká in the Hall of Fame, the announcement of the new stadium alongside Inter, interviews to staunchly defend Ruben Amorim, and above all, the desire to continue improving his AC Milan 2.0 starting… in January.

“Yes, because the Rossoneri’s post-derby signals are about building, not just about exaltation. This is where we need to start again, laying the foundations for a different, fierce, and winning Milan, like the one seen in the derby, which clearly can’t be enough.”

“And the first announcement will be that of the new Head of Football: Milan has a sealed verbal agreement with Markus Krösche, the man who has done a great job at Eintracht Frankfurt in recent years, both in scouting talent and capital gains, ready to take over the Rossoneri project.

“Krösche will be active for the January transfer window and will be in direct contact with Cardinale regarding the Rossoneri’s new plans.

“He’s a figure generating enthusiasm at Casa Milan, having already been the first choice since last June: Cardinale preferred to wait a few months to have his priority rather than fall back on managers who weren’t first choices. Now, the Krösche era is about to begin.”

“Milan’s objectives? It’s going to be a busy January: the defender could and should have arrived at the end of August, but there was no timeline or method. Milan has reinstated Tomori, but at least one defensive reinforcement is already planned for January.

“The favourite since June has been Sporting’s Gonçalo Inacio, but Milan has at least three other options on the list and has recently also sent Sylla of Union St. Gilloise to scout. It might not end there: keep an eye on the attack, where an additional option to give Gonçalo Ramos a rest shouldn’t be ruled out if the right opportunity presents itself.

“Assessments about Franceso Camarda will be made in the coming weeks, but Milan is exploring the transfer market and will continue to surprise. At least one signing, likely two. And then… the transfer market will dictate inspiration, ideas, and innovations.

“With new players and a Rossoneri that has never been so fired up in recent years.”

For the first time in a while, it’s a continued stream of positive news for Milan, which is only a good thing.

#1903. Chelsea injury news: Emiliano Martinez, Moises Caicedo update provided ahead of Sunderland game

By Darren Plant | 06 Nov 2026 15:15, Last updated: 06 Nov 2026 15:15

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has suggested that goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez could return from injury to face Sunderland on Sunday.

The Blues are currently preparing to make the trip to the Stadium of Light sitting in fourth place in the Premier League table.

However, despite last weekend's 2-0 victory over Manchester United, Alonso has several selection dilemmas, including one involving Martinez.

Having suffered a fractured jaw against Everton in the middle of October, the Argentina international has been replaced by Mike Penders.

Despite the young Belgian stopper making a positive impression, Alonso said at a press conference on Friday that Martinez was in contention to start in the North-East.

When quizzed on the 34-year-old's condition, Alonso told reporters: "Tomorrow we have our last training session before Sunday and we will decide but he is training well."

He added: "All of the decisions are tough. But it is good that Emi has made a great effort to be back and ahead of the plans to be part of the team.

"Tomorrow we will check and Sunday we will take the final decision."

Meanwhile, Alonso hinted that Moises Caicedo was a major doubt with an issue picked up versus Man United.

The Spaniard said: "He had a little problem after the last game so we expect to check on him tomorrow. It is a discomfort more than the calf."

While Penders would have understood his role at Chelsea at the start of the season, impressing against Liverpool and Man United should have changed the situation.

Although we are not quite at the "passing of the touch" moment, Penders showed in that double-header that he is ready to take his chance.

Whether Alonso agrees with that notion remains to be seen, but logic suggests that it makes more sense to keep with Penders on Sunday than rush Martinez back from a serious injury.

#1902. Rangers turn up heat on leaders Celtic despite controversy in Paisley

A bitterly cold, damp Saturday night in Paisley yielded precisely the sort of calculated, business-like victory that defines title credentials. Under the floodlights of the Marbill Coaches Stadium, Rangers maintained their pursuit of league leaders Celtic with a dominant 2-0 win over St Mirren.

In truth, the scoreline scarcely reflected the visitors’ control of proceedings, a superiority anchored by a dominant midfield display and punctuated by goals from Ryan Naderi and Dan Neil in either half.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

This was an exercise in efficiency for Rangers manager Derek McInnes as his side arrived in Renfrewshire looking to maintain their unbeaten away record in the league this season. Making just one change from last weekend’s Premier Sports Cup semi-final triumph over Aberdeen, his side displayed a fluid composure that left the hosts chasing shadows for long periods.

Although Rangers have endured an inconsistent record on previous visits to Paisley, dropping points in three of their last four league outings, their latest success extended a domestic unbeaten run to 12 matches and left them in a confident place heading into the final international break of the year.

St Mirren, under the stewardship of Craig McLeish, had promised a robust, positive approach as they looked to arrest a worrying slide in form that had saw them lose six of their previous eight games. However, the reality for the Buddies was an evening spent largely in a low defensive block, starved of possession and unable to test Ivor Pandur in the visitors' goal until it was too late.

The breakthrough arrived in the 18th minute through a moment of controversy. Left-back James Penrice drove into the penalty area and went down under pressure from a trailing Samuel Ramos leg. While the home support vociferously claimed the new Scotland call-up went down theatrically, referee Nick Walsh pointed directly to the spot.

Naderi stepped forward, ignored the jeers, and showed admirable composure to confidently dispatch the penalty into the bottom right-hand corner, with Jacob Chapman diving the opposite direction. It marked the German’s sixth goal in his last seven games.

Going behind did little to alter St Mirren’s conservative shape as their build-up play lacked urgency, and Rangers continued to dictate the tempo. Their front three of Badredine Bouanani, Kim Minsu, and Kevin Kelsy probed intelligently. The hosts did have a penalty appeal of their own dismissed when Ramos’ header back across goal appeared to strike Naderi’s hand.

The second half followed an identical script, and the definitive blow arrived just after the hour mark. It was a goal engineered by the persistent work of Kelsy who battled fiercely to pick up Olwethu Makhanya’s pass.

His determination allowed the ball to break kindly to Neil, restored to the starting line-up, on the edge of the box and the midfielder side-footed effort took a wicked deflection of Declan John to completely wrong-foot the helpless Chapman, with the ball nestling in the bottom left-hand corner. It gave Rangers some welcome breathing room.

St Mirren did mount a late, spirited assault on the visitors goal, but were denied on several occasions by Pandur. Their best opportunity fell to substitute Eseosa Sule, who met a pinpoint cross from John at the back post. It seemed a certain goal, but the Croatian goalkeeper produced a sublime reaction save to preserve his clean sheet.

Ultimately, McInnes’s men navigated the closing stages with a minimum of fuss, starving the hosts of the ball and suffocating any remaining glimmers of a late comeback. The victory keeps them firmly within striking distance at the summit, a solitary point behind reigning champions Celtic with a game in hand still to play after this weekend.

#1901. Leeds United 1 Spurs 0: Okafor the hero as intense, in-character second half ends winless streak

Shortly after being serenaded after coming on in the final quarter at Elland Road, he took care of Spurs in the here and now.

The fact that three substitutes all combined will not have been missed by Daniel Farke, who misses nothing.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

A throw-in from Melvin Bard was won by Dominic Calvert-Lewin with the ball dropping to Harry Wilson, who had the presence of mind to spot Okafor, who gave Rodrigo Bentacur the slip before firing home confidently on 77 minutes.

And that was that as Leeds produced an intense, in-character second half to secure a first win in six matches and head into the international break in improved mood. A fourth win in a row for the first time in over 1,000 days continues for Spurs.

The win was not without controversy, that said.

It took a big moment on 37 minutes to set pulses truly racing among home punters in an otherwise pretty uneventful first half.

A lengthy VAR check saw the Stockley Park overlords scrutinise Jayden Bogle’s challenge on Mathys Tel for a considerable length of time before it was deemed not to be serious foul play.

Tel was left writhing in agony after being caught on the back of his Achilles by Bogle’s left foot. It looked accidental as opposed to intentional and the video decision-makers concurred, although it could easily have gone the other way and resulted in a red card.

Tel managed to carry on for a few minutes before eventually making way.

The other incident of note also involved technology with an early check resulting in a non-penalty award for Leeds after a cross caught Mateus Fernandes’ shoulder. The Spurs midfielder’s arm was outstretched, but it was rightly deemed as not intentional.

Headline team news from a home perspective saw Lucas Nmecha and Longstaff handed first league starts of the campaign, with Harry Wilson and Dan James dropping to the bench.

You had to go back to last November for the previous time that Longstaff stepped out from the off at Premier League level.

Spurs-wise, ex-United favourite Archie Gray switched to midfield following the recall of Pedro Porro at right-back.

Gray received a few jeers whenever he touched the ball. Spurs had some half-decent moments in transition and had the better of it in open play and more control - with Fernandes seeing plenty of the ball in particular. Leeds displayed perspiration, but little inspiration.

Spurs’ best moments arrived midway through the half. An incisive move down Leeds’ right ended in Omar Marmoush’s low shot taking a slight, but important touch off Tarik Muharemovic before James Trafford gathered. The deflection took the sting out of it.

Mohammed Kudus also tested Trafford low down, with the Leeds keeper having no first-half dramas unlike seven days earlier.

Leeds, who started nicely enough, huffed and puffed. One chance arrived ahead of the break but Nmecha’s downward header was easily claimed by Antonin Kinsky.

Leeds made a change at the interval, with Melvin Bard coming on for Gabriel Gudmundsson, presumably due to an injury concern.

Attacking the Kop, Leeds produced a dangerous moment with Van de Ven getting a key clearance in front of goal after Bogle whipped in an excellent low centre.

Longstaff’s left-wing corner yielded the hosts best moment up to press.

Calvert-Lewin directed a header towards goal and Dominic Solanke got an important block. The Leeds striker helped the ball back into the danger zone, with Nico Elvedi nodding wide.

United, attacking the Kop, were starting to up it and soon missed a golden chance after Tanaka and Longstaff led the break.

Calvert-Lewin did well to evade van der Veen and teed up Tanaka, who ballooned an excellent chance over.

Nevertheless, Leeds were the ones in the ascendancy and Spurs were starting to look flustered all of a sudden. Indicative of that was a triple change just before the midway point of the half from Roberto De Zerbi.

One flash of life - in relative isolation -from the visitors saw one of the substitutes in Conor Gallagher fire a shot just wide. Most of the action was towards the other end. Nmecha hit a post, but the flag was instantly raised before Calvert-Lewin fired over, soon followed by Bogle.

Leeds continued to knock on the door, with Kinsky forced into significant work to tip over Longstaff’s hooked effort in splendid fashion.

The pressure was sustained and the Kop sucked one in. Trafford made a key late save to deny Van Hecke.

Farke said: "There's no replacement for this winning feeling after such a game in the dressing room. It's great to have this winning feeling back.

"All the credit and all my compliments go to the boys' terrific performance against a really in-form Tottenham side.

"You could see in the first half that they would go with confidence also into this game. For us, of course, a difficult period because we're missing - since a few weeks more or less - in training and also in the starting line-ups, some key players like Anton Stach, Noah Okafor and for Dominic (Calvert-Lewin). It’s not the easiest spell with several injury problems.

"It was important today to show this unity and commitment. We were technically spot on in order to avoid all their processes and all their individual quality in order to score goals and reduce them to very, very little already in the first half.

"We were missing a bit in our game (in the first half) in our final third was again the quality of the crosses and the finishing pass was perhaps not there, but I think in the second half there was no doubt just one team was pushing."

On the impact of Okafor, who had been struggling with an abductor issue, he continued: "Credit to our medical department and also to Noah, he has worked in a very, very disciplined fashion, 24 hours a day more or less to be available.

"Yesterday with a few concerns of the medical department, they said: 'Boss, Listen, if you want to use him, you have to make sure that you stay unbelievably disciplined and you can't bring him on longer than 15 or 20 minutes, this is what the muscle can't handle (more minutes). But if you want to do this and Noah feels also right, then yeah, perhaps you can do this.' He took part yesterday in parts of our team training."

Farke confirmed that Swedish international Gabriel Gudmundsson came off with a hamstring injury at the break, with Bard coming on and performing excellently in his place.

He said: "Gaby had problems with his hamstring, so it was not possible for him to keep going. I always prefer to have Gabby available but don't get me wrong, but I had a good feeling straight away because Melvin had his best week in training since he was together with us.

"He could feel that he has momentum and I was not for one moment concerned when I had to throw him in. I hope that it's not too bad with Gaby and I hope to have him back on the other side of the international break, but also credit for Melvin.

The win was not without controversy, that said.

It took a big moment on 37 minutes to set pulses truly racing among home punters in an otherwise pretty uneventful first half.

A lengthy VAR check saw the Stockley Park overlords scrutinise Jayden Bogle’s challenge on Mathys Tel for a considerable length of time before it was deemed not to be serious foul play.

Tel was left writhing in agony after being caught on the back of his Achilles by Bogle’s left foot. It looked accidental as opposed to intentional and the video decision-makers concurred, although it could easily have gone the other way and resulted in a red card.

Tel managed to carry on for a few minutes before eventually making way. He left the stadium on crutches after the game.

Farke said: "I haven't watched the scenes back and didn't have the chance, so for that I can't give a clear opinion on it. I would need to watch it back. The scene with Jayden was not too far away from my bench, I think it looked a bit like a very unlucky coming together.

"Of course sadly for Mathys that he was injured, and of course fingers crossed that he's back pretty soon. But it felt a bit like there was not too much speed in this action, and what I can guarantee is Jayden Bogle is one of the most fair players in the whole country.

"He's too much sometimes for me like a butterfly and not like an eagle anyhow, so soft in a positive way. What I can guarantee is that he would never ever injure a player on purpose, or not even foul a player on purpose, because he's a great character."

Spurs chief Roberto De Zerbi had no complaints about the result and felt his side's second-half performance lacked 'personality'.

He said: "It was two games in the same game. In the first half, we had clear chances to score and didn't suffer.

"In the second half, I don't know why, we suffered too much and deserved to lose game. We didn't win any duels and one-on-one's. There was space to play, but we didn't take the right positions and didn't show personality and who we are.

"I don't want excuses. We have to be honest, if we are not honest today, the future is not good. I was surprised as my players worked very well this week. We spoke all week about the intensity and type of game we would find in this stadium. It was not a surprise for us."

On the incident regarding Tel, he added: "I can't say something more because I didn't clearly see the situation.

"I was surprised, because in the same position in the second half, there were two different fouls and two yellow cards (offences) on Pedro Porro.

"I don't know if it was a red card or not on Mathys Tel, but for sure Pedro Porro, it was a yellow card. Why I'm telling it like this, because the parameter of the referee was not good enough, I think, for these both situations."

#1899. Liverpool's £123m Bradley Barcola problem: Iraola under scrutiny

By Naim Beneddra | 06 Nov 2026 15:17

Bradley Barcola's difficult start at Liverpool has raised questions about whether Andoni Iraola is making the best use of the French winger, with the manager himself acknowledging a significant difference in the player's performances depending on his position.

The 24-year-old arrived from Paris Saint-Germain in August in a deal worth up to £123m, but has struggled to reproduce the consistency that made him one of Europe's most exciting attacking talents.

His three Liverpool goals have all come in the same Champions League match against LASK, while he has contributed two assists in the Premier League. Thirteen appearances into his Anfield career, the return remains modest given the expectations surrounding his arrival.

However, Barcola's struggles cannot be explained by his finishing alone. He has featured in several attacking roles under Iraola, including an unfamiliar central position during Wednesday's 3-2 Champions League defeat to Fenerbahce.

The Spanish coach's subsequent assessment has brought a wider tactical question into focus: why has Liverpool's expensive summer signing spent so much time away from the position in which he is most effective?

Iraola's decision to deploy Barcola as a central striker in Istanbul was partly influenced by the availability of his other attacking players.

With Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz starting on the wings, Alexander Isak was initially kept on the bench, having been earmarked for a shorter appearance.

Liverpool's manager believed Barcola's acceleration could cause problems for Fenerbahce's defenders, particularly when attacking the space behind their back line.

"We thought it would work well because I think Bradley, in terms of speed and the match-ups, it could be good for him," Iraola explained after the defeat.

However, he acknowledged that the experiment had not produced the same attacking threat as some of Liverpool's more familiar combinations.

"All season he has been better when he has played outside wide," Iraola admitted.

The assessment was revealing, particularly given Barcola's preference for operating on the left.

Of his 13 Liverpool appearances, six have come away from that preferred position, including five on the right and Wednesday's experiment through the middle.

Barcola's greatest strengths are his acceleration, close control and ability to isolate defenders in one-on-one situations. On the left, he can receive the ball facing an opponent, accelerate into space and create opportunities with either a cutback or a direct run towards goal.

Operating centrally presents a different challenge.

Against teams defending with limited space between their centre-backs, he is required to receive more frequently with his back to goal, hold off defenders and make decisions in congested areas.

Those demands do not necessarily suit a player whose most dangerous actions often begin with a run from a wider position.

Iraola has not ruled out using him through the middle again, insisting that such an arrangement could be useful against particular opponents.

Nevertheless, Liverpool's attacking performance in Istanbul offered little evidence that it should become his regular role.

Isak scored after replacing Ngumoha in the second half, while the Reds were more threatening once they had greater presence in central areas.

Barcola has also been guilty of individual errors that cannot be attributed to his positioning.

Against Brentford, for example, he attempted an unsuccessful chip when through on goal and later lost possession after delaying a pass during a promising counter-attack.

His decision-making and finishing therefore remain legitimate areas for improvement, regardless of where Iraola selects him.

There are mitigating circumstances surrounding Barcola's arrival that help explain his uneven performances.

Liverpool agreed to pay PSG an initial £106m, with a further £17m in potential add-ons, making the Frenchman one of the most expensive signings in the club's history.

Yet the transfer was completed only towards the end of August, depriving him of a full pre-season with Iraola and his new teammates.

Barcola had also been involved in the World Cup during the summer, leaving him with limited preparation before adapting to a different league and a new tactical environment.

His first Liverpool appearance came in early September, following several weeks without competitive football.

The physical demands of the Premier League have presented another adjustment, while Liverpool's difficulties against compact defensive teams have not always allowed Barcola to exploit the space that made him so effective at PSG.

There is also the challenge of developing an understanding with teammates who are themselves adapting to Iraola's methods.

In an exclusive interview with Sky Sports, published before the Fenerbahce defeat, Barcola acknowledged that he had yet to reach his best level.

"No, I don't think I'm at my best yet," he admitted. "You still haven't seen the best version of me."

The Frenchman believes improving his relationship with those around him will be crucial.

"On top of that, we're working with my team-mates so that they can make the most of my strengths," he explained.

"So yes, I think once we really develop that understanding, things will get much better."

Barcola's comments suggest that he recognises the need to improve without regarding his difficult start as evidence that the transfer has failed.

Nor does he consider his fee or the responsibility of succeeding Mohamed Salah to be an additional burden, insisting that he wants to establish his own identity at Anfield.

The challenge for Iraola is to find an attacking structure that helps him do so.

Ngumoha and Munoz have provided encouraging alternatives on the flanks, while Isak and Cody Gakpo offer different qualities through the middle. Those options give the Liverpool manager flexibility, but also complicate the task of establishing a settled role for Barcola.

The Reds travel to Crystal Palace on Sunday, when Iraola will have another opportunity to reconsider his attacking selection following the defeat in Turkey.

Barcola must improve his finishing and decision-making if he is to justify Liverpool's investment. But with his manager openly acknowledging that he performs better out wide, how consistently he is allowed to operate in that position will be an important part of assessing his progress.
